scenes.text: This is a living room in Liberty, Kentucky, one month after the Green River came through it. You can still see the water line on the wall.
In Belfry, Kentucky, Carrie Charles's walls were stripped to the studs. In Ponce, Puerto Rico, Luz Maldonado spent her days cleaning out a friend's house.
Every one of these families has to do the same thing next: prove what they lost, on a form, while everything is still wet.
Between 2016 and 2018, FEMA found one point seven million applicants ineligible. One of the most common reasons was missing evidence of the damage.
And while families wait, the scammers arrive. Fake relief websites. Fake agents. Fake fees. Post-disaster fraud cost Americans an estimated nine point three billion dollars in 2023 alone.
That's why we built Sheltr. Safe shelter for storm survivors, and for the agent that helps them.
A survivor takes a phone photo of the damaged room. That's all we ask of them.
Inside a sealed sandbox on Vultr, Sheltr rebuilds the room in 3D, in metres, from that single photo.
Then the agent finds the damage and writes its own measuring code. When that code fails, it reads the error and tries again. Every attempt is on screen.
Six damage items, pinned to the exact spot in the room, each with a measurement and a repair estimate.
Now the dangerous part. The survivor gets a text: claim your relief payment in 24 hours. They ask Sheltr to check the link.
The page forces a download onto the device. Then it tries to send the survivor's data to an outside server.
The sandbox holds. Both threats contained, inside a browser micro V M that lives for six seconds and is then destroyed. The survivor gets a plain verdict: this is a scam.
Then Sheltr fills in the aid application, step by step, with a vision check on every screenshot. Nothing is submitted until the survivor reads it and taps approve.

Under the hood: two machines on Vultr. The control plane holds every key and never runs untrusted code. The sandbox host runs each task in a fresh micro V M with its own kernel and no network, then destroys it. Blast radius zero.
This is real. A real FEMA photo, end to end through the public URL: a 3D room, five damage items, an estimate, three sandboxes started and three destroyed, in thirty-four seconds.
After the storm, the hardest part shouldn't be the paperwork. Sheltr. Built on Vultr, at Agent Arena 2026.
